title: Quiet Badge
statement: A workshop records the lowercase letter printed on each arriving attendee badge in the string badges. Return the zero-based position of the earliest arrival whose badge letter appears exactly once in the complete record. Return -1 if no badge letter is unique. An empty record also returns -1.
constraints: badges contains only lowercase English letters a through z.

examples.explanation: a and b each appear twice. c is the earliest letter that appears once, at index 3.
Every recorded badge letter occurs more than once.

hints.content: A letter can look unique early in the record and appear again later.
Separate learning how often letters occur from choosing the earliest arrival.
Store a frequency for each badge letter.
Count the complete record, then scan its positions from left to right.
Return the first index whose letter has frequency one; otherwise return -1.

testCases.explanation: a and b each appear twice. c is the earliest letter that appears once, at index 3.
Every recorded badge letter occurs more than once.
Only y occurs once, at index 2.
Both b and c are unique; b arrived earlier.

solutions.title: Count around each arrival
solutions.intuition: An arrival qualifies only when its letter has exactly one occurrence in the entire record.
solutions.approach: For each position, count that position’s letter in the full string. Return the first position with count one.
solutions.pseudocode: For each index i: count occurrences of badges[i]; if count equals one return i; return -1.
commonMistakes: Returning a letter before reading the whole record can miss a later duplicate.
Returning an arbitrary unique map entry can ignore the required arrival order.
solutions.interviewExplanation: I count every badge letter first, then scan the record in its original order. This preserves the earliest-arrival requirement while avoiding a full recount for each position. Two linear scans are O(n), and the fixed alphabet bounds the map size.

solutions.title: Count once, choose once
solutions.intuition: The same frequency can answer the uniqueness question for every occurrence of a letter.
solutions.approach: Build one frequency map. A second scan follows arrival order and returns the first index with frequency one.
solutions.pseudocode: Count every letter in a map; scan indices in increasing order; return first letter with count one, else -1.
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(1), because there are at most 26 distinct letters
